goal_text: I've already built an LLM app and want to understand agents

nodes.title: What makes an agent different from a chain?
nodes.one_liner: The core shift: model decides its own next steps, not you

nodes.title: The agent loop
nodes.one_liner: How reason → act → observe → repeat actually runs in code

nodes.title: Giving your agent tools
nodes.one_liner: Defining, exposing, and calling tools the model can invoke

nodes.title: Parsing and executing tool calls safely
nodes.one_liner: Handling model output, running actions, feeding results back

nodes.title: Managing state and memory across the loop
nodes.one_liner: What to carry between steps and how to keep context sane

nodes.title: Controlling the loop: stopping, retries, guardrails
nodes.one_liner: Termination, error handling, cost/step limits, avoiding runaway loops

nodes.title: Wire an agent into your existing app
nodes.one_liner: Where the loop lives, async, streaming, surfacing progress to users

nodes.title: Debugging and observing agent behavior
nodes.one_liner: Tracing steps, catching bad reasoning, iterating on prompts

outline.rationale: The user is a builder who already knows LLM prompting/chaining and wants to ship one agent into a real app. I skip LLM fundamentals and framework surveys entirely. Node 1 anchors the conceptual delta (autonomy/control flow) they specifically need since they only know chains. Nodes 2–6 decompose the buildable core of a single agent: the loop, tool definition, tool execution, state/memory, and control/guardrails — these are MECE-ish (concept, then each distinct implementation concern). Nodes 7–8 handle integration into their existing app and the practical reality of debugging, which matters for actually shipping. I deprioritized multi-agent orchestration and library comparisons per the confirmed understanding, keeping depth at "enough to design and implement."
